title: Heat Storms Explained: Supersized Heat Waves Now Cover the Planet for Months
excerpt: A Reuters analysis of hourly temperatures since 1960 defines heat storms as heat waves covering at least 1% of the globe — and finds they have risen from about five a year in the 1960s to about 102 a year this decade.
body:
• A Reuters investigation analysing hourly temperatures since 1960 has defined a new category — the heat storm: a heat wave that at its peak covers at least 1% of the globe, roughly half the size of Canada.
  • Heat storms averaged about five a year in the 1960s; this decade they average about 102 a year, and at least one has been active continuously since July 6, 2008.
  • The largest on record, named Vera, lasted 367 days in 2023-2024 and swept across almost 85% of the globe.
  • Staying safe in extreme heat: treat five or more days of abnormal heat as a sustained emergency — hydrate before you feel thirsty, avoid outdoor exertion in peak afternoon heat, check on elderly neighbours, and seek cooled spaces, as heat is estimated to kill almost half a million people a year.

India knows heat waves well — weeks of 45-degree afternoons are a familiar part of summer. A Reuters investigation published on October 20 argues that the planet now faces something larger, and has given it a name: the heat storm.

Reuters consulted two dozen meteorologists and climate researchers and analysed temperatures for every hour of every day since 1960, across more than one million grid squares covering the globe. Its reports are available at Reuters and in its account of the largest heat storm on record.

What a heat storm is — and how it differs from a heat wave

A heat wave and a heat storm are the same phenomenon at different scales. Reuters defines an ordinary heat wave conservatively, as five or more consecutive days of abnormally high temperatures — daily highs in the hottest 10% of the historical range for that place. A heat storm is a heat wave that grows so large that, at its peak, it covers at least 1% of the Earth's surface, about 5.1 million square kilometres, roughly half the size of Canada. At that point Reuters names it, as forecasters name tropical storms and hurricanes. The distinction is therefore size and reach, not a different kind of weather: a heat wave is local or regional and lasts days; a heat storm is continental to global in footprint and can persist for months, merging with, splitting from and cascading into other heat storms across oceans and hemispheres.

"Naming events is a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening."

— Anthony Leiserowitz, Director, Yale Program on Climate Change Communication

From five a year to 102 a year

Heat storms were rare in the 1960s, averaging about five active storms a year. This decade they have averaged about 102 a year. The largest heat wave of the 1960s reached about 6% of the planet over 46 days; the largest this decade, Heat Storm Vera, lasted 367 days across 2023-2024 and swept over almost 85% of the globe, touching virtually every human being on Earth.

Over the same period, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has risen by more than 30%, and the average portion of the planet likely to be covered by heat storms and heat waves has risen more than 12-fold. A cascade of consecutive or simultaneous heat storms that began on July 6, 2008 has still not stopped: for more than 18 years, at least one heat storm has been active somewhere on the planet.

Why this matters for India

For India, the finding reframes a familiar risk. A local heat wave is already dangerous; a heat storm means the same extreme heat can sit over far larger regions for far longer, straining power grids, water supplies, outdoor work and public health systems simultaneously rather than district by district. Reuters notes heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year globally. The investigation also found the world is currently in Heat Storm Raimundo, which began on February 28, 2026 and has since touched almost three-quarters of the planet's surface.

What happens next

Reuters has built a live Heat Storm Tracker so readers can follow named storms in real time. For households, the practical lesson is duration: plan for heat that lasts weeks, not days — store water and medicines ahead of forecast heat, shift outdoor work to early morning, and treat persistent night-time heat, which prevents the body recovering, as a warning sign to seek medical help for dizziness, confusion or stopped sweating.
